Valuations are relatively attractive, but macro risks should be taken into consideration, such as public finances, a volatile peso, and potentially lower FDI in light of recently passed judicial reforms. Central Bank Credibility Remains a Concern
extracted_context.summary_text: Turkey Inflation Refresh March 2019 Impact of Using Consensus Inflation on Turkey Inflation Assumptions The impact of using 2 years of consensus inflation is meaningful for Turkey’s long term average inflation In effect, the 10 year average of 10% is now obtained using a long term estimate of around 8.5%-9.0% The somewhat changes the scope of the estimate and allows us to focus more on what type of number we truly think can be achieved over the long run Turkey CPI Weights 3 Source: Turkish Statistical Institute Historical Success Analysis of Different Regimes Average CPI Median CPI Average Deviation from Target Median Deviation from Target Implicit Inflation Targeting 2002-2005 23.4 17.3 4.6 2.2 Inflation Targeting 2006-2018 9.1 8.7 3.9 3.7 Post GFC Policy-Integrating Financial Stability 2011-2018 9.3 8.5 4.3 3.5 Erdogan Era 7/2014-2018 10.5 9.2 5.5 4.2 Inflation Targeting ex 2017/18 2006-2016 8.3 8.2 3.0 3.1 Post GFC Policy ex 2017/18 2011-2017 7.9 7.8 2.8 2.8 Erdogan Era ex 2017/2018 7/2014-2016 8.0 7.9 3.0 2.9 Central Bank Credibility Remains a Concern It is important to note that while central bank credibility has been an issue for a while in Turkey, the expanded powers given to the executive in 2018 further damaged the ability of the CB to be an independent arm In 2018, President Erdogan claimed the exclusive power to appoint central bank rate-setters and named his son-in-law as overseer of economic policy. This follows several years of departures from his investor friendly team. As part of his election in 2018 that expanded his powers, he promised to take more control over monetary policy. He has repeatedly stated that he believes that keeping borrowing costs low is a priority and that higher rates actually lead to higher inflation. While the central bank did raise rates aggressively in September, 2018 (from 17.75 to 24), Erdogan was critical of the move and let the world know that his patience with these types of moves was limited. Many believe that the current move towards relative orthodoxy is a temporary one.

From a top-down perspective, valuations and profitability are above our long-term assumptions, creating a negative reversion that will impinge future expected returns. On the other hand, Japan equities are fairly valued from a bottom-up perspective based on our analysts’ cash flow outlook. In general, Japan equities present a balanced risk/reward profile. Japan equities are moderately unattractive, with the current P/E ratio slightly above our long-term assumption at 16 times. Current higher profitability is expected to normalize and contribute to a negative valuation reversion over the next decade. ( see Slide 32 for details). We are neutral on Japanese equities from a bottom-up perspective. Our coverage is trading at around a fair valuation. Non-software companies caught in the SaaS sell-off are priced for even lower terminal growth, with some effectively priced as if they will go out of business. Confidential — For Internal Use Only Data: FactSet, MIM as of 31 March 2026 SBC impact on implied terminal growth rate ECTIVE Stock-based compensation is not a cash item; therefore, most technology companies report Non-GAAP financials that exclude SBC expense. We believe SBC should be treated as a cash expense, as companies are required either to dilute shareholder value by issuing stock or to buy back shares from the market using cash. For companies exposed to high AI risk, SBC could become less attractive, and employees may demand higher cash compensation. Subtracting SBC from free cash flow results in a higher implied terminal growth rate. Confidential — For Internal Use Only Data: FactSet, MIM as of 31 March 2026 Software-System Software-Application Non-Software Implied terminal growth rate (SBC adj) ECTIVE Once adjusted for SBC, there is some heterogeneity in software terminal valuations. Korean Equity Market is Heavily Weighted in the Technology Sector, with Heavy Stock Concentration
extracted_context.summary_text: Multi Asset Research Asia Equity Research MIM EMEA Korea Conviction Update September 2025 Korea is moderately unattractive from an asset class level perspective, while it is fairly valued from an MER perspective, leading to an overall score of Medium. Korea is heavily weighted in the Technology Sector, and has extremely large stock concentration, greater even than the US and UK, with the top 10 stocks making up almost 60% of the index, and Samsung alone represent close to 30%. When considering macro or country economic news (such as corporate governance) it is worth noting the stock specific nature of the index may drive returns more than these aggregate events. Korean returns and fundamentals are also becoming more idiosyncratic relative to global fundamentals. Related to the above, we find that the returns are not well explained by their sector exposure. We also find Korean returns and fundamentals are becoming more idiosyncratic relative to global markets. Large stock specific risk that Samsung loses market share given the rapid increase in Chinese memory expertise. Corporate governance reforms in July 2025 to increase shareholder rights increased market optimism. However, it is still too early too see if this will lead to any real positive improvement, and we further estimate that the upside from corporate governance to be in the region of c.1% expected returns. In terms of potential portfolio considerations, we find cash flows are more sensitive relative to global equities than most DM’s, increasing cyclicality risk. Prices have since rebounded from Nov 2023 as 10-yr interest rates have fallen meaningfully. The Reits sector has been out of favour as a sector as interest rates have risen and rising risks to a number of property sectors ie office, residential and retail. According to Morgan Stanley’s broker research team, net flows to US real estate funds have been consistently in net outflow since late 2021. Fundamental Risk Medium Contingent risks score points to (the low end of) Medium. When combined with the Systematic Risk trend assessment, this remains at a Medium score. Conviction Medium While some Reit sectors and regions are out of favour others are in-favour by investors, with office out of market favour while industrial is in market favour. Europe has taken on significant debt and will likely incur value destructive equity raises but the US and UK are likely to avoid any material dilutive raises. Investors have rotated away from Reits due to rising interest rates and due to the risks of economic growth slow down. Ultimately, we are guided by our valuations which show a medium. Earnings growth continues to be modest, with a subdued rental outlook in major markets. Fundamentals: Earnings growth has been assisted by lower debt funding costs, residential development profits, and increased funds management earnings. As has been the case for several years, property rental growth over the last year was fairly muted, and it is not expected that this will change in the next few years. Recent strength in property valuations appear to be driven more by cap rate compression than rental growth. Property valuations look less attractive from a dividend yield perspective and a range of valuation metrics (P/E, P/NTA and cap rates). Strong interest from offshore buyers for Australian commercial property assets has been driven by low offshore funding costs, relatively high cash yields compared to international assets, and the fall in the AUD. 2. Previous updates highlighted the potential upside from telecoms offering convergent services. It is possible that it may take longer for the true benefits of this strategy to play out, but we suggest a healthy dose of scepticism here given the current data. We also wanted to stress some of the structural difficulties the telecommunication services industry faces, with large government ownership stakes and limits on cost structures on top of regulatory intervention limiting the competitive advantages of these business and their returns. extracted_context.summary_text: US SMID Conviction Update April 2025 CMA Team Executive Summary Executive Table Executive Summary US Small Caps have different key sector drivers than large caps, with Financial Services, Industrials and Consumer Cyclicals accounting for the majority. They also have lower international revenue exposure and less concentration. We find sector exposure can explain a large proportion of the returns of US Small Caps. However, there has been a divergence YTD, suggesting a more idiosyncratic driver over this shorter period, which we find is coming from sentiment rather than fundamentals. In terms of fundamentals, we find the absolute levels of profitability are lower. Growth, on the other hand is higher and this is what drives the higher PE. We find US Small Caps are more sensitive to macroeconomic variables compared to Large Caps. While we find no evidence of an unconditional small cap premium, we see strong evidence that buying at attractive valuation levels will lead to high forward returns. Small caps are neutral from a top-down asset class perspective and moderately attractive from a bottom-up aggregation approach. Our higher price-to-earnings assumption is mainly driven by strong growth expectations, despite the relatively weaker fundamentals including ROE and PM than Large caps. At the stock level, equity analysts maintain a positive outlook, albeit the coverage ratio is low. Combined with our neutral view on market sentiment. There is elevated risk of disruptive changes to business models with negative impact across a number of areas. extracted_context.summary_text: December 2017 EM Financials Why are we looking at this sector? 2 EM FN is the second largest sector by market capitalisation accounting for approximately 24% of the MSCI EM index. EM FN’s VIR are high, making it a relatively attractive investment opportunity. This supports the overall EM VIR. Since the GFC, EM FN’s assets have grown rapidly and concerns over these assets’ quality have been raised. This has been led by the Chinese government’s large stimulus package to boost external demand. The implications of our current assumptions, was that EM FN’s P/B deserved to trade at a sizeable premium to DM FN book values. We needed to get some comfort around this. Key points 3 Chinese banks have not been immune to poor lending. Government helped tidy up the mess in the late 1990s/ 2000s. The Chinese government is well aware that it needs to reduce the risks building up in the domestic financial system. Following the GFC, government initiated a stimulus package, with formal bank credit used as the distribution mechanism. Alongside the formal bank loans, money from the informal sector was funnelled through financial institutions. This statement by the PBOC governor certainly emphasises the risk in the system: “ China’s financial sector is and will be in a period with high risks that are easily triggered. Under pressure from multiple factors at home and abroad, the risks are multiple, broad, hidden, complex, sudden, contagious, and hazardous. The structural unbalance is salient; law-breaking and disorders are rampant; latent risks are accumulating; [and the financial system’s] vulnerability is obviously increasing. [China] should prevent both the “black swan” events and the “gray rhino” risks.” Government will look to tighten liquidity, encouraging more market determined credit allocation and remove the protection that inefficient SOEs enjoy. Despite strict lending standards, Chinese banks used loopholes to grow off-balance sheet debt. WMPs is one such shadow banking product that has ballooned, investing in a variety of assets. extracted_context.summary_text: February 2016 CMA Assumptions Summary BRICS EM CMA returns are substantially different from the current DAA returns. Payouts largely in order – with the exception of Korea and Mexico. Suggestions: Use long-term payout adjusting for repurchase yield. China, India and Indonesia’s GDP per capita growth is excessive compared to my view of the shareholder return experience (China – dilution and India – share class difference / family ownership) Suggestion – use sector trend per share Sector margins for most EM countries are more consistent with long-term earning trends. I do not think that country sector margins can remain as high as they currently are, without further competition. Suggestion – Switch to sector margins for Brazil, China, India, South Africa and Indonesia Placing these changes into the model, revised CMA returns Brazil, China, India and Indonesian returns fall by approximately 1.5% - 4%.
